0401-1500s.title: Chronological History of the Sixteenth Century
0401-1500s.cleanTitle: Chronological History of the Sixteenth Century
0401-1500s.creditLine: Image courtesy of the Internet Archive. Digitized by the Library of Congress.
0401-1500s.caption: The four chronological charts included in Elizabeth Palmer Peabody’s Chronological History of the United States (1856), which display the significant events of the 1500s, 1600s, 1700s, and 1800s. Images courtesy of the Internet Archive. Digitized by the Library of Congress.
0401-1500s.altText: One of Peabody’s four chronological charts showing the significant events of the sixteenth century. The chart is a 10-by-10 grid (100 squares for 100 years), and the year 1565 has multiple sub-squares shaded in, highlighting the year’s prominence.
0401-1500s.altTextLong:
One of the four chronological charts included in Elizabeth Palmer Peabody’s Chronological History of the United States. This chart shows the significant events of the sixteenth century. The chart is a 10 by 10 grid, for a total of 100 squares, each representing one year of the century. The chart is read from left to right and from top to bottom such that the year 1501 corresponds to the top left square and 1600 corresponds to the bottom right square. Each square is further divided into nine smaller squares, the position of which represents a specific type of event, according to the following key: 
 
Top left: Battles, Sieges, Beginning of War
Top center: Conquests, Annexations, Unions
Top right: Losses and Disasters
Middle left: Falls of States
Middle center: Foundations of States and Revolutions
Middle right: Treaties and Sundries
Bottom left: Births
Bottom center: Deeds
Bottom right: Deaths, of remarkable
individuals
 
An event is indicated by shading the appropriate sub-square in the appropriate year. The color of the shading indicates the country that is involved. In the chart of the sixteenth century, the chart is mostly unshaded, with only one or two events per row (decade). The most prominent set of events occurs in 1565, in which multiple sub-squares are shaded. There is no key to the colors included in this image.

0412.title: Visualizing Time
0412.artist: Tanvi Sharma, Dan Jutan, and Jay Varner
0412.creditLine: Design by Tanvi Sharma. Prototype by Dan Jutan. Final implementation by Jay Varner.
0412.caption: An interactive version of Peabody’s chart in which event squares can be cross-referenced with their description. Below, the same event squares are visualized in timeline form. Design by Tanvi Sharma. Prototype by Dan Jutan. Final implementation by Jay Varner.
0412.altText: A screenshot of the interactive version of Peabody’s charts. On the left is the original version of the chart. On the right is a contemporary re-creation. Below is a timeline with each event sub-square stacked in its appropriate year.
0412.altTextLong: One of Peabody’s original charts is placed to the left of a digital transcription of the same chart. A timeline of the years depicted on each chart, of which there are four for the user to choose from (the sixteenth, seventeenth, eighteenth, and nineteenth centuries), stretches beneath both the original and digital charts, with the option for the user to click on various squares distributed along the timeline as a bar graph. The user can hover over the squares either on the bars of the timeline or within the chart, and the corresponding square on the other be highlighted as well. For instance, if the user drags their mouse over the first square within the bar for the year 1728 on the timeline, the square on the digital copy of Peabody’s chart will also light up. Peabody’s key that indicates event type lies beneath the timeline, and each number also lights up when the user hovers over a particular square.
0412.cleanAltText: A screenshot of the interactive version of Peabody’s charts. On the left is the original version of the chart. On the right is a contemporary re-creation. Below is a timeline with each event sub-square stacked in its appropriate year.
0412.cleanAltTextLong: One of Peabody’s original charts is placed to the left of a digital transcription of the same chart. A timeline of the years depicted on each chart, of which there are four for the user to choose from (the sixteenth, seventeenth, eighteenth, and nineteenth centuries), stretches beneath both the original and digital charts, with the option for the user to click on various squares distributed along the timeline as a bar graph. 0423-willard-temple.title: The Temple of Time
0423-willard-temple.creditLine: Image courtesy of the David Rumsey Map Collection, Cartography Associates.
0423-willard-temple.caption: Emma Willard’s perspectival Temple of Time (1846). Image courtesy of the David Rumsey Map Collection, Cartography Associates.
0423-willard-temple.altText: A chart that depicts a Roman temple in a highly perspectivized, quattrocento style. Each column as well as the ceiling, floors, and walls are labeled with the name of an important ruler. At this scale, few individual events can be discerned.
0423-willard-temple.altTextLong:
A historical chart that depicts a Roman temple in a highly perspectivized, quattrocento style. Each column is labeled with the name of an important ruler. US rulers are in the foreground on the left, and European rulers are in the foreground on the right. Behind those are additional columns with the names of Roman, Greek, and biblical rulers. The columns get smaller as they recede into the back of the chart, indicating that those rulers date earlier in time. At the very back of the temple, written on the wall, are the words “The Creation.”
 
On the ceiling of the temple are the names of additional sets of historical figures: statesmen, philosophers and discoverers, theologicians, poets and painters, and warriors. They are arranged in keeping with the perspectivized style, such that the more contemporary figures appear larger and towards the front, and more historical figures appear smaller and towards the back. On the floor are channels that correspond to different countries, with relevant events written out. A palette of pastel colors separates each country’s channel from the others. These same colors shade the columns and the ceiling, resulting in an overall impression that is visually and textually dense. At this scale, few individual events can be discerned.

0423-willard-temple.cleanAltTextLong:
A historical chart that depicts a Roman temple in a highly perspectivized, quattrocento style. Each column is labeled with the name of an important ruler. US rulers are in the foreground on the left, and European rulers are in the foreground on the right. Behind those are additional columns with the names of Roman, Greek, and biblical rulers. The columns get smaller as they recede into the back of the chart, indicating that those rulers date earlier in time. At the very back of the temple, written on the wall, are the words “The Creation.”
 
On the ceiling of the temple are the names of additional sets of historical figures: statesmen, philosophers and discoverers, theologicians, poets and painters, and warriors. They are arranged in keeping with the perspectivized style, such that the more contemporary figures appear larger and towards the front, and more historical figures appear smaller and towards the back. On the floor are channels that correspond to different countries, with relevant events written out. A palette of pastel colors separates each country’s channel from the others. These same colors shade the columns and the ceiling, resulting in an overall impression that is visually and textually dense. At this scale, few individual events can be discerned.

0428-clarke-1-4000BC-ps-30x43-2.title: Chart of Scripture
0428-clarke-1-4000BC-ps-30x43-2.caption: A vertical timeline created by Anne Laura Clarke as it was displayed on her traveling lecture tour. Photo courtesy of Granville Ganter.
0428-clarke-1-4000BC-ps-30x43-2.altText: An antique chronological chart that lays out a vertical timeline organizing various ancient civilizations and empires into parallel colored columns, spanning from 4000 BCE to the time of Christ. The chart is mounted between two wooden rollers.
0428-clarke-1-4000BC-ps-30x43-2.altTextLong: An elaborate timeline printed on a worn scroll, which hangs open against a door. The timeline is composed of bars of varying widths that stretch varying lengths down the chart, each representing the major civilizations Clarke chose to track against the prominence of the birth of Christianity, which is represented by the central and largest bar, colored in blue. Carthage, Rome, Macedonia, Greece are the civilizations that fall to the left of the blue bar, and Phoenicia, Egypt, Assyria, Lydia, Syria, Persia, and China reside on the right.
